summary:
SPHEREx Cosmic Detective is a public web tool that makes SPHEREx’s all-sky infrared data easy for anyone to explore. Enter any RA/Dec (decimal or sexagesimal), choose a field of view and detector band, and the app pulls the SPHEREx exposures covering that patch from NASA/IPAC IRSA. It removes zodiacal light, aligns every exposure onto one north-up grid, co-adds them by epoch, and plays them as a blink video so moving objects stand out.

Going beyond the brief, an Epoch Gallery & Change Dashboard compares each epoch with the previous one in side-by-side, swipe and difference views. It automatically flags movers (with displacement, speed and direction) and brightening or fading sources, with light curves, a SIMBAD “already known?” check and CSV export. Spectra are generated on the fly, and every view is deep-linkable by URL for embedding.

It matters because most known comets and brown dwarfs were found by volunteers blinking images. This tool turns a billion-object dataset into something a curious person can scan in minutes, and it picks up new data releases automatically.
details:
SPHEREx Cosmic Detective lets anyone look at a patch of sky in SPHEREx data. A user enters RA/Dec, field of view (2–15′) and a detector band. The backend then does the following:

  1. It queries NASA/IPAC IRSA (TAP) for every SPHEREx exposure covering that position.
  2. It downloads small FITS cutouts through IRSA’s cutout service.
  3. It subtracts the modelled zodiacal light.
  4. It reprojects each exposure, using its TAN+SIP WCS, onto one common north-up grid.
  5. It co-adds the exposures into time epochs, optionally for one detector band.
  6. It serves the epochs as images that play as a blink video.

For the Change Dashboard, each epoch is differenced against the previous one and smoothed with a PSF-sized matched filter. Noise is measured from the data, and peaks above a chosen sigma are found. A negative lobe paired with a positive lobe is a mover, reported with displacement, speed and direction. An unpaired lobe is a brightening or fading source, reported with a light curve. Spectra are built on the fly with aperture photometry, taking each wavelength from the file’s WCS-WAVE table. A SIMBAD cross-match checks whether a candidate is already known.

Benefits and intended impact

The tool turns a billion-object dataset into something a curious non-expert can scan in minutes. It points experts toward real candidates, such as brown dwarfs, comets and variable stars. Because it queries IRSA’s live tables, new SPHEREx releases appear without code changes. Every view is deep-linkable (?ra=&dec=&fov=&band=), so it can be embedded in other sites and citizen-science projects.

Creativity

  • The epoch gallery with side-by-side, swipe and difference views turns “blink comparison” into an investigation.
  • Movers are detected automatically from their dipole signature.
  • Spectra are generated on demand.
  • Voyage mode, a 3D tour of SPHEREx-visible objects, draws newcomers in.

Tools and technologies

Next.js, React and TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Three.js, Framer Motion and Recharts. The backend is Node route handlers with a custom FITS reader (image and binary-table extensions), WCS/SIP reprojection and a PNG encoder. Data comes from the IRSA TAP and cutout services and SIMBAD TAP. No special hardware is needed.

Factors we considered

  • Different wavelengths: each SPHEREx exposure is at a different wavelength, so apparent variability can come from the wavelength mix changing. The dashboard offers per-band comparison and warns users, and moving-object detection is robust to this.
  • Noise and false alarms: a sensitivity control sets the detection threshold.
  • Transfer time: the field of view is user-selectable, and results are cached.
  • Access: a keyboard-friendly, reduced-motion-aware interface with plain-language explanations.
  • Offline fallback: the app falls back to sample data if the archive is unreachable.
